articles.headline: "Hold Me While I Larf!"
articles.text:
"Hold Me While I Larf!"

[Cut of a crowing rooster.]

SING, BROTHERS, SING!

Where, oh where is the Dickinson Freight Route?
Where, oh where is the Dickinson Freight Route?
Where, oh where is the Dickinson Freight Route?
Sunk, now, in a gumbo slough!
articles.summary: A rooster cartoon and mock verse crowing over the rival Dickinson freight route to the Black Hills.

articles.headline: More 'Whistling to Keep Up Courage.'
articles.text:
Dispatches from St. Paul state that Messrs. Pennell and Jones have signed contracts for 17,000,000 pounds of freight from Chicago, St. Paul and Minneapolis via Little Missouri crossing to the Black Hills. Jones will put on seventy-five teams, Pennell forty-five and Larson forty as a starter. Immediate arrangements will be concluded, however, to enlarge the transportation facilities. The stage and mail line will also be put on as soon as possible. Most of the bullion product of the Black Hills mines has also been contracted for and will be taken over our line instead of the old Pierre line as formerly. Last year Deadwood's carrying trade was 40,000,000 pounds. This year it will doubtless go over 50,000,000 pounds.

We wonder if our citizens fully realize what the success of this route means. It means success for the town and every person in it. It means a large number of new citizens. It means new houses and new stores. It means one of the largest circulating mediums of any town on the line. In itself it means all this. Were it not for the freight route, there would surely have been a large and flourishing city here. With it, it means a flourishing city from the start. The capital and labor will be here first and these will draw a large number of citizens. The start given it by the freight route will receive a fresh impetus by its being made the cattle headquarters of a large extent of territory and doubtless in a short time the headquarters of the whole Northwest.

At the present time there is no point on the line between Mandan and Helena, and we think can safely say between Minneapolis and Portland, which has as large a cash backing as this point. There is an abundance of money and Marquis de Mores has shown that he is not all afraid to spend his share in anything to increase the general welfare. We do not need to create a boom here. It is already upon us. The next year will witness such an improvement as will astonish even the most sanguine. At least twenty-five letters have been received at The Cow Boy office alone from persons thinking of settling here. The success of our freight route will be the deciding point. They and hundreds of others will see the advantage of coming here and our little town will soon be alive with the bustle of incoming citizens.
articles.summary: Reports freight contracts by Pennell and Jones for 17 million pounds of Black Hills freight via the Little Missouri crossing and boosts Medora's prospects and de Mores' backing.

articles.headline: Meeting of Bad Lands Stockmen.
articles.text:
The proceedings of the meeting held at Little Missouri in Pennell & Roberts' hall, Thursday afternoon, Feb. 28, are as follows:

The meeting was called to order at 2 o'clock by Howard Eaton, who nominated Mr. B. Barr for chairman. There being no other nominees, Mr. Barr was declared unanimously elected. In the same way A. T. Packard was elected secretary.

Appropriate remarks were made by the chairman as to the purpose of the meeting. He showed plainly the need of organization, and his words met the approval of all present.

Mr. J. L. Truscott stated as the reason for the absence of several cattle men that they thought it was only a meeting to organize for the round-up and also that the river having risen so much it was almost impossible to get here.

The secretary moved, and Mr. Eaton seconded the motion, that a committee of four, including the chairman, be appointed to draw up an order of business. The chair appointed Messrs. Packard, Eaton and Truscott. Pending their report a recess of ten minutes was held.

The meeting being again called to order, the report of the committee was read by the secretary.

The first article was, "That this meeting be considered as only preliminary to a meeting held on a date to be decided by a call committee." Carried.

"The object of this article is that no definite steps should be taken at this meeting for a Bad Lands organization. Many of the most prominent cattle men are absent owing to the impossibility of getting here, and all should fully understand the object of the meeting beforehand and have a voice in its organization."

The second article was, "That a committee of five be appointed to call a meeting for the organization of the Bad Lands cattle men, to report at that meeting a constitution and by-laws and any other business to come up for consideration for the governing of the above association when organized." Carried, with an amendment by Mr. Eaton that the chairman of this meeting be appointed on the committee. The chair appointed Messrs. Eaton, Packard, Merrifield and Paddock four members of the committee, himself constituting the fifth.

The third article was, "That a committee of three be appointed to draw up a call for the organization of a Territorial association. Carried, with the understanding that the chair should appoint three influential men on the committee and notify each man of his appointment, and instruct them to draw up the call.

The last article was that a list of names should be prepared of the men interested in cattle anywhere in this vicinity. The following list was obtained: Dickey Bros., Stoneville; Clark & Plum, Spearfish; Driscoll & Son, Spearfish; Hughes & Simpson, Stoneville; Continental Cattle Co., Stoneville; Towers & Gudgell, Keith, Mont.; Berry, Boice & Co., Keith, Mont.; Gregor Lang, J. L. Truscott, Wm. Dantz, Bullion & Marsh, D. K. Wade, J. L. Roberts, Ferris & Merrifield, E. W. Casey & Co., Marquis de Mores, E. G. Paddock, Wm. Tuttle, Custer Trail Cattle Co., Soho Cattle Co., Wadsworth Bros., Geo. Fitzgerald, Little Missouri Land & Cattle Co., all with their postoffice at Medora, Dak.; Grisy & Wibaux, D. C. Rowe, Morrison & Davis, of Keith, Mont.; J. A. Cotton, Griffin & Ward, Keystone Cattle Co., John Heffron, W. O Serrine, Moore & Rumsey, George McCone, of Glendive, Mont.; Capt. Wm. Harmon, Bismarck; T. R. Selmes, Mandan; Andrew Messersmith, Dickinson; Fair & Darling, Terry, Mont.; Richardton & Co., Richardton; J. Coulson, Belfield. The above list was gotten up hurriedly and probably contains many omissions. The secretary made a call on every one to send in for publication the names of all cattle men who would be interested in a Territorial organization.

Adjourned.

B. BARR, Chairman.
A. T. PACKARD, Secretary.
articles.summary: Minutes of the Feb. 28 preliminary meeting of Bad Lands stockmen at Pennell & Roberts' hall, naming committees and listing area cattle men.

articles.headline: A Question for Teller.
articles.text: Little Rock Special: Advices from the Texas border represent that stockmen are making an effort leading to congressional action in the matter of establishing a permanent cattle trail running from the line of that state via Kansas and Indian Territory to the west. Some time ago the cattle men addressed a memorial to Secretary Teller asking him to use his authority to prevent the closing of what is known as the Western trail, which runs through lands belonging to the Cheyenne-Arapahoe agency in Indian Territory, and which lands have been leased for a term of years to a syndicate of sotckmen and inclosed with fences. It is understood that Mr. Teller has given the memorial consideration and that the trail will be kept open this season at least. The lessees state that the fence is so arranged that herds can be passed through the lands without trouble. However the question of a permanent trail is a serious one to to the stock-growing interest of the south-west. The shipping of stock to the western markets and ranges is owing to the high freight charges and distance from railroads, impracticable in most cases The difficulty in passing herds over the present trail is likewise great in Kansas and elsewhere. Settlers have taken up lands along the trail and given herdsmen trouble by claiming damages for trespass and for water. The drive this year is expected to foot up many hundred thousand head and next season will probably double that number. In view of the immense pecuniary interest involved, it is deemed advisable to have congress locate a permanent trail, thus giving a guarantee to stock growers that there will be no obstacle in the way of getting stock to western markets. It is believed that all the stock associations in the country will take action in the matter, and that a vigorous and concerted movement will be made on congress to secure the desired trail.
articles.summary: Clipped Little Rock dispatch on Texas stockmen seeking a permanent national cattle trail and Secretary Teller's handling of the Western trail.

articles.text: The worst storm of the season has been raging here for the past three days, and poor stock will no doubt feel the effects severely. A fierce wind has been blowing from the north and northwest since Monday, accompanied by snow, with hail occasionally for a variation. Tuesday morning the thermometer showed three degrees below zero and yesterday — degrees. While the snow is a stem-winder and no mistake, we do not anticipate any considerable loss of stock from the fact that the bulk of the stock is still strong and able to endure a very hard racket.—[Medicine Lodge, Kan., Cresset.
articles.summary: Clipped Kansas report (Medicine Lodge Cresset) of a three-day storm on the range.

articles.headline: SPORTING NOTES.
articles.text:
Hanlan has left San Francisco for Australia.

The rowing event of England, the Oxford-Cambridge eight-oared race, will come off April 5.

Schaefer has returned from France. It is undecided when his next game with Vignaux will take place.

Every betting agency in Paris is being closed by the city authorities by reason of complaints of cheating.

If we are not mistaken, the fastest mile on ice was trotted recently at Ticonderoga, N. Y., by Ella Dale in 2:14.

The chances are good for a race this summer between Teemer and Hanlan. If the race comes off, it will create more excitement in rowing circles than any race for years.

The recent cushion-carom billiard match at St. Louis, between Eugene Carter and Tom Gallagher was won by the former. Score, 400 to 327; Carter's average, 4 32-92; Gallagher's average, 3 54-91.

The National Trotting Association was started in 1870 in debt and with fifty-one members. In the last six years it has awarded $4,208,599.32 in purses and stakes. There are now 219 members and $6,000 in the treasury.

Bubear's recent victory over Elliott in England, leads a Referee correspondent to think that he is the best sculler England has ever produced. His form is described as wonderfully like Hanlan's and it is considered that he will give the champion a close race.

Feb. 24, at Galveston, Tex., Mrs. Nellie Burke accomplished the difficult feat of riding one hundred miles in five hours. The race was for a wager of $1,000. Altogether she made forty changes and won the race in the remarkable time of 4 hours and 55 minutes.

A colored sculler named Charles Reynolds has made the fastest time over the Paramatta river champion course at Sidney, Australia. The course is 3 miles and 331 yards straight away. His time was 20 minutes and 6 seconds. The best previous time was 20 minutes and 44 seconds. Another break in the record.
articles.summary: Column of national and foreign sporting paragraphs (rowing, billiards, trotting), clipped exchange matter set in the paper's own type.

articles.headline: ON THE RANGE.
articles.text:
The Idaho Register says that stock in that part of the country is as fat as butter and requires no feeding.

At a meeting of the stockholders of the Converse Cattle Company, held last Saturday, all the shares being represented, the capital stock was increased from $550,000 to $1,000,000. The calves on the range grow so rapidly that it keeps the owners busy to keep up with them.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

Mr. Charles Wheeler has sold to E. Johnson and Wm. Parker his ranch and about 3,000 head of stock. The property is among the finest in Colfax county and includes a fine range. The purchase makes the parties owners of about 10,000 head of stock. The price paid is understood to be $85,000.—[Colorado Live Stock Journal.

A delayed correspondence from Fort Laramie, dated the 4th, which reached here the 9th, says the snow has all gone and the grass is green. Cattle on the range are looking well. The Laramie river is open and cattle get plenty of water. The only fatalities heard of are three or four calves dying from black leg. The outlook is very promising.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

The calf crop will be an average one—neither light nor heavy in numbers, a trifle better though on account of more and better bulls being on the range than heretofore. To inquiring minds wishing to know how stock are wintering in Texas we can safely say they are doing well, better than average. Losses none to speak of. Certainly not from bad weather or shortness of range.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

The Durbin Land and Cattle Company filed articles of incorporation at the office of the secretary of the territory and county clerk yesterday. The incorporators and officers are: John H. Durbin and Thomas F. Durbin, of Cheyenne; Godfrey Snydacker, Morris Rosenbaum and Joseph Rosenbaum, of Illinois. The principal office will be in Cheyenne. Capital $750,000, paid up in full.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

Stockmen in the northern part of the State fear the late heavy snow and cold weather will result in the loss of cattle. The ranges around Pueblo, and in fact anywhere south of the divide, are exempt from this danger. We sometimes lack sufficient moisture during the winter and spring to insure good grass, and stock does not take on flesh so fast as in colder localities, but we never lose any cattle by heavy snows and cold weather.—[Pueblo, Colo., Star.

The Messrs. McDowell, of Hunnewell, have taken the safe plan this winter of carrying their poor cattle through. They drove their cattle from below last summer, held them on the range till after frost, then cut out all the poor ones and drove them into the State, where they are feeding them hay and millet and running them in stalk fields. By this plan they are safely carrying their herd through with very slight loss. They expect to save the lives of enough cattle to pay all expenses of the feeding, etc., and have all their cattle in good shape for the summer.—[Caldwell, Kan., Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped range paragraphs from western stock journals (Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, Texas, Kansas).

articles.headline: Our Stock Interests.
articles.text:
Hon. J. B. Grinnell, of Iowa, recently prepared and sent on to the press an extensive paper on "Legislation for the Suppression of Contagious Diseases Among Animals." The document was lengthy and well loaded down with arguments and statistics which were calculated to show the importance of maintaining cleanliness and purity of our meats. He gave the following "head-line" facts, which give one some idea of the magnitude of our cattle interests:

1. There is an investment of $1,008,000,000 in cattle, as estimated by the department of agriculture, representing 41,171,000 animals. That of swine is $291,000,000, representing over 43,000,000 animals.

2. The losses annually on exportation of cattle and beef, consequent upon restrictive regulations and the decreased relative consumption of our beef, aggregate many millions of dollars. We reach an approximate estimate by these facts relative to our foreign trade as follows:

The exports of 1880-81 were 368,463 animals; those of 1882-83 were 212,551—a loss of 155,000 animals, and in value a loss of $11,506,000 in two years.

The exports of fresh beef for two years were less by 50,071,167 pounds and by value $2,191,190. The value of pork products decreased in the same time to the extent of $35,679,093.

This shows a falling off of about $25,000,000 per annum for two years, as compared with the receipts for the preceding years.

No nation has so large a relative portion of its wealth in domestic animals, and none can show such strides in material advancement during the present century. But what is our foreign trade? The exports of provisions from the United States during the last fiscal year were in value about $107,000,000; those in 1882 amounted to $120,000,000, equal to a falling off in a single year of $13,000,000. Our exports of manufactured articles for the last year aggregate $211,000,000 against $103,000,000, a gain of $108,000,000 in a single year. It was a reasonable expectation that our animal exports would have increased in like ratio as the manufactures, which would have enhanced the value of all domestic animals and furnished, instead of a mortifying fact, a proud exhibit.

The causes of a decline are not found in high prices at home nor in inferior products; rather in suspicion of diseases and the clamor of interested parties, which led to arbitrary restrictions, oppressive quarantine regulations and forbidding beeves which were ripened for the highest markets to pass beyond the shambles, and the egress of young premature cattle on the English pastures. Pork products up to the Chicago meeting were prohibited by France, and they are inhibited now from Germany, our long-time valuable customer. It was their whims, caprices, jealousies, commercial restrictions and bans which decreased our exports and led the commissioners of agriculture to call the Chicago meeting of November.

That convention developed facts and was fruitful in results. That there were solitary cases of pleuro-pneumonia and limited to the eastern border states, that western herdsmen had just cause of alarm on account of the shipment of young stock west from the narrow pastures and dairy districts of the east. It was shown that across the ocean there was a morbid appetite for suspicions and facts that would justify severe restrictions and an absolute inhibition of our products.

The cattle commission formed by the treasury department gave decided opinions and imparted valuable information, but were constrained to admit that they were powerless in an emergency to stop the spread of contagious diseases, and that it was a vain hope there would be an increased foreign demand for our cattle and meat without radical congressional enactment.

Who can be indifferent in the face of our great perils and recounting the losses by foreign restrictions? We are emphatically a nation of beef eaters, and by the extent of our domain and beautiful climate are justly entitled to the honored designation of the first producer among civilized nations. It is the question of healthful food for the masses, of profitable tonnage for the railways and of deep concern in cultivating fraternal relations abroad, not less than a question for the political economist in maintaining a good trade balance sheet. If we can impress our congressional delegation with the necessity of early and decisive legislation we shall have accomplished a noble work and have earned the warm commendation of millions of citizens whose interests have been neglected and whose vocation and property have been imperiled.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped Northwestern Live Stock Journal piece summarizing J. B. Grinnell's paper on cattle disease legislation and falling U.S. meat exports.

articles.text: The hide and pelt business of Colorado and New Mexico last year amounted to $2,500,000. Colorado had by far the greater number of hides, while New Mexico excelled in the matter of pelts. The goat skins of New Mexico alone amounted to $300,000.
articles.summary: Clipped note on the Colorado and New Mexico hide and pelt trade.

articles.text: The Ogalalla Land and Cattle company have just purchased the Bosler herd of cattle, numbering from thirty-five to forty thousand head, paying $1,250,000. The Ogalalla company is a new outfit but has unlimited capital and is now one of the largest outfits on the range. [Sidney P.-Telegraph.
articles.summary: Clipped Sidney Telegraph note on the Ogalalla company's purchase of the Bosler herd.

articles.text: A stock company has been formed to run a pony express from Deadwood to Belfield, Billings county, on the Northern Pacific.
articles.summary: Territorial-news paragraph (patent inside) on a pony express company planned from Deadwood to Belfield.

articles.text: A company has recently been organized in Bismarck, to be known as the Bismarck Loan and Trust company, and it will commence business within a few weeks. The officers are Frank B. Allen president; Marquis de Mores, vice-president; R. B. Mellon, treasurer, and Frank La Wall, secretary. Capital, $100,000.
articles.summary: Territorial-news paragraph (patent inside) naming the Marquis de Mores vice-president of the new Bismarck Loan and Trust company.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores will return in about a week.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores is expected back in about a week.

articles.text: Read the report of the cattle meeting and send in your list of cattle men.
articles.summary: Readers are asked to send in names of cattle men.

articles.text: Howard Eaton has been shipping in lumber for a large stock barn which he will soon erect on his ranch.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton is shipping in lumber for a large stock barn on his ranch.

articles.text: Mrs. McNanny, sister of E. G. Paddock, has gone to Minneapolis to have her eyes treated. She expects to return soon.
articles.summary: Mrs. McNanny, E. G. Paddock's sister, has gone to Minneapolis for eye treatment.

articles.text: Frank Chase, of the Killdeer mountains region, was in town and will start back to-morrow with Mr. Clark, who intends visiting him for a short time.
articles.summary: Frank Chase of the Killdeer Mountains was in town and returns tomorrow with Mr. Clark.

articles.text: Large preparations have been made for the dance at the Pyramid Park hotel to-morrow evening and it will doubtless be largely attended. All are invited.
articles.summary: A dance is planned at the Pyramid Park hotel tomorrow evening.

articles.text: Edwin Bulpin has resigned from the region of owls and man-slides for one of jack-rabbits, in other words, for Idaho. Hugh Flynn, of Mandan, takes his place.
articles.summary: Edwin Bulpin has left for Idaho; Hugh Flynn of Mandan takes his place.

articles.text: Wm. Smith, cattle inspector for Montana, was here last Sunday. He had been in pursuit of some thieves and came here to see about the Marquis' ponies stolen recently.
articles.summary: Montana cattle inspector Wm. Smith came to Medora about the Marquis' recently stolen ponies.

articles.text: As many of our friends can testify, Mr. Kline sent that box of cigars and the "De Mores," as the new brand is called, is already an established favorite. The cigars will soon be on sale.
articles.summary: Mandan cigar maker Kline's new "De Mores" brand will soon be on sale.

articles.text: Rev. Cooke, of Gladstone, held two services last Sunday at the Cantonment. His preaching was able and well received. We hope Mr. Cooke will make it convenient to come here often.
articles.summary: Rev. Cooke of Gladstone held two services at the Cantonment last Sunday.

articles.text: A cow-boy here was being catechised by a minister and gave some rather unique answers. In reply to the question "What is the noblest work of God?" he replied, "THE BAD LANDS COW BOY."
articles.summary: A joke about a cowboy naming the Cow Boy as God's noblest work.

articles.text: The best specimens of gypsum we have yet seen were brought in and added to our collection by Frank Smith. The Smith Brothers alone, if they keep on, will give us a splendid collection by fall.
articles.summary: Frank Smith added gypsum specimens to the Cow Boy's collection.

articles.text: Frank Coughlan started for New York last Saturday. He is firmly impressed with the advantages this country possesses for young men and will return as soon as possible. He left two Indian arrows with us as mementoes.
articles.summary: Frank Coughlan left for New York last Saturday, intending to return.

articles.text: J. H. Rising, who has filled the position of night operator for some time past, has gone home to Hillsdale, Mich. Mr. Rising was a general favorite, and we are sorry to lose him. Mr. Harris, of Dickinson, takes his place here.
articles.summary: Night operator J. H. Rising has gone home to Michigan; Mr. Harris of Dickinson replaces him.

articles.text: John Keefer handed us a rib of a beef that is certainly an anatomical curiosity. The rib has been broken and over-lapped but it is almost impossible to see the line of knitting on one side. On the other the bones are separated half an inch.
articles.summary: John Keefer brought in a curiously healed beef rib.

articles.text: The "Sankey" part of the gospel firm came in yesterday for repairs or something. He says that the "Big-foot" Ryder gang have cut 1500 posts and hauled them to the bank of the river. Their "everlasting fortunes" are just in sight.
articles.summary: The 'Sankey' of the 'gospel firm' reports the Ryder gang has cut and hauled 1,500 posts.

articles.text: Several visitors called during our visit to Belfied the first of the week. Our sorrow at this fact, however, is wonderfully tempered by the remembrance of the pleasant evening spent with Mrs. Fred Ertel and Miss Nellie Dailie, at Belfield.
articles.summary: The editor visited Belfield early in the week.

articles.text: If the Northern Pacific road is noted for one thing more than another, it is for the good qualities of the hotel men along its line. One of the best of them is Max Bass, of Belfield. Max is a thorough hotel man and is also a boomer from way back on the beauties of Belfield.
articles.summary: Praise for Belfield hotel man Max Bass.

articles.text: The boarders at the Hotel de Mores all unite in thanking Mr. Z. Hyde for the prairie chicken dinner for which he furnished the chickens this noon. That all of them were shot with a rifle, some of them being on the wing, sufficiently testifies to Mr. Hyde's skill as a marksman.
articles.summary: Z. Hyde furnished rifle-shot prairie chickens for a Hotel de Mores dinner.

articles.text: J. A. Ferris started for Mandan last Saturday to buy a stock of dry goods. He will open soon and will doubtless be successful in his venture. Mr. Ferris is widely known as a reliable man and under his administration there will not be a repetition of the "Wall street failure!"
articles.summary: J. A. Ferris went to Mandan last Saturday to buy dry goods for a store he will soon open.

articles.text: The sad news came in yesterday morning that J. L. Truscott's father had died the day before in New York. Mr. Gibbs started immediately for Mr. Truscott's ranch. The news, though not personal to any one here, will strike all with a feeling of sadness as Mr. Truscott has endeared himself to every cattle man in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: News arrived that J. L. Truscott's father died in New York; Mr. Gibbs rode to Truscott's ranch.

articles.text: Mr. W. E. Bean, of Mt. Sterling, Ky., writes us a valuable letter concerning blooded stock and also encloses copy for an advertisement which will be of interest to our cattle men, and is found in another column. Mr. Bean is an old and experienced breeder and an enthusiast on blooded stock. Questions addressed him by our stockmen would probably bring out many valuable points.
articles.summary: Kentucky breeder W. E. Bean wrote about blooded stock and placed an ad.

articles.text: For any tourist who has visited the Bad Lands to say that he does not know Frank Moore and the Pyramid Park hotel is to argue himself unknown. In view of the certain boom which has already struck this point, every effort is being made to receive the influx of visitors which will come during the warm season. The Pyramid Park hotel will receive a thorough overhauling and every convenience will be added for the comfort of visitors. Many additions will be made, new rooms added and everything will be strictly first-class. Mr. E. G. Paddock will run a livery stable in connection with the hotel and every facility for viewing the wonders of the Bad Lands will be at hand. We are glad to notice this new departure and do not doubt that it will have every success.
articles.summary: Frank Moore's Pyramid Park hotel will be enlarged for tourists, with E. G. Paddock running a livery.

articles.text: Joe Pennell is still in St. Paul.
articles.summary: Joe Pennell remains in St. Paul.

articles.text: Bob Roberts went to Bismarck on the early train yesterday morning.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts went to Bismarck yesterday.

articles.text: W. B. Milne, of the popular dry-goods house of Wyman, Mullin & VanDyke, of Minneapolis was in town yesterday and to-day. Mr. Milne is one of the boys and has made many friends since his arrival. He has the "cinch" on the dry-goods trade here. We hope he will come this way often.
articles.summary: Minneapolis dry-goods salesman W. B. Milne was in town.

articles.text: It was more fun than a basket of monkeys to hear Arthur Smith yell: "By the bald-headed Mackinaw," as he took a header off his wagon and struck out for a bale of hay that had fallen into the Little Missouri and was floating toward the big Muddy amid the drifting ice at the rate of [ten?] miles an hour. He got the hay but haysn't dried out yet.
articles.summary: Arthur Smith plunged into the icy Little Missouri after a bale of hay.

articles.text: More than one heart will be struck with sorrow at the bereavement that Mr. and Mrs. Osterhaut have just endured. The little baby which had made itself a general favorite by its infantile beauty, died this morning. As Mr. Osterhaut moved up the river last week, it was impossible to learn more than the mere fact of the death and that it was entirely unexpected.
articles.summary: The infant of Mr. and Mrs. Osterhaut died unexpectedly.

articles.text: Our citizens have labored under one disadvantage which they will endure no longer. There has been no insurance agent here and great difficulty has been found in obtaining insurance. We wish to state that we have just received a commission as agent for the old reliable Springfield Ins. company, one of the best if not the best in the U. S. All insurance matters will be promptly attended to by writing to or calling at the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office has become agent for the Springfield insurance company.

articles.text: Jack Simmons, better known as "Black Jack" made Medora a flying visit yesterday. He is fresh from the Coeur D'Alene gold region. He reports great scarcity and costliness of provisions and much suffering on account of the snow. The gold regions as yet, are an experiment but he thinks the prospects are good. At any rate so many people will go in this spring and summer that it will be a good point for merchants and lumbermen. He has a saw-mill near the mines and will get to work with it as soon as possible.
articles.summary: "Black Jack" Simmons, back from the Coeur d'Alene mines, visited Medora.

articles.text: The list of names published in our report of the cattle meeting is doubtless very incomplete. We wish every reader of The Cow Boy who knows any additional names would send them in immediately. It is necessary to get a full and complete list of all cattle men in the territory and those who will be actively interested in a Territorial organization. This would include many in Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Minnesota and Iowa. All who know additional names will facilitate the work of the committee and confer a favor on the editor by sending them to The Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Appeal for more names of cattle men for a Territorial organization.

articles.text: The meeting of stockmen held last Thursday did all that a full attendance of every man in the Bad Lands could have accomplished. It started the ball rolling that will eventually make this point the cattle headquarters of the Northwest. We do not care to go over the arguments again to proove this, for it is so manifest on its face. There is no argument against it and everything is in its favor. The bulk of the work now rests with the two committees. Upon these rests in a great measure the responsibility of making this point what it should be. Every member should realize the importance of his position and let no personal matters interfere with the performance of his committee duties. The report of both committees will probably be published in our next issue.
articles.summary: Editorial on last Thursday's stockmen's meeting and the duties of its two committees.

articles.text:
A Miles City special says that it is reported there that a remarkable death rate prevails among Marquis de Mores' sheep in the Little Missouri Bad Lands in Dakota, the result of poison. The Marquis has some enemies. Sheep on Montana ranges are healthy. The Marquis lost 6,000 out of 12,000. It can be accounted for on no other ground than that poison was administered by enemies of the Marquis, on account of the killing of O'Donnell last year.

The above article, clipped from The Evening Missourian, is too foolish even to contradict, were it not for the fact that it has been extensively copied and commented on by editors who should know more than to give it credence. The only and true reasons for the death of the sheep, as we stated in our last issue, were that they were fall-clipped, belonged to the Merino breed, were shipped in late in the fall and were entirely unacquainted with the ranges till after the snow flew. These are the reasons and none other for the death of the sheep. The long-wooled variety, shipped in at the same time, are doing as well as cattle.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy rebuts a Miles City report that de Mores' sheep were poisoned, blaming fall clipping and late shipment of Merinos.

articles.text: Mr. Gregor Lang's herd of cattle, fifty miles up the river, are a standing advertisement for the Bad Lands and the best one they have ever had as a cattle country. They are mostly young cattle and were brought in here during the intense cold of January. On the way here they suffered severely from the effects of a railroad accident, many being hurt badly and all bruised more or less. On the day of their introduction to this country the thermometer was 48 degrees below zero. For about three weeks they were close-herded and fed on hay about five miles down the river. At the end of that period they were branded deeply and driven to the ranch up the river. Since that time has come some very cold weather, enough to test the endurance of old range cattle. These were mostly young cattle entirely unused to range life. They have not had a spear of hay fed them, they were driven upon a new range and branded deeply during the worst weather we have had, and not a solitary head has died from exposure. More than that, they are all fat and in good condition. There is no cattle country under the sun that can show a record like this. It is simply wonderful. When the cattle were driven on the range bets were freely offered that before spring was over half the herd would be dead and there were no takers. Do our readers wonder now why we desire to advertise the Bad Lands by our name and that we are proud to do so?
articles.summary: Gregor Lang's young herd, brought in at 48 below in January, has wintered without a loss.

articles.headline: BELFIELD GOSSIP.
articles.text:
BELFIELD, Dak., March 4, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

As Belfield has not yet been represented in The Cow Boy, will you permit your humble scribe to transmit the following few pointers in regard to this rising young town:

Belfield, although in its incipiency, is one of the most thriving and picturesque towns of the West Missouri country. Its population to-day numbers about 200 persons, which will double ere spring has fully set in. It is the center of as truly handsome an agricultural country as any portion of the "great and glorious Northwest" can boast of. In regard to productiveness it stands pre-eminently without a superior. Its close proximity to the Bad Lands admirably adapts it to successful stock raising. Lignite coal, of a very superior quality, is obtainable on almost every claim merely for the digging. One of the marked features of the town is the substantial manner in which its buildings have been erected, it sporting the finest residences of any town on the line.

The business community is composed of a fine hotel, general store, lumber yard, real estate office, saloon, postoffice and grocery. Among other improvements contemplated is a furniture factory, brick yard and elevator.

Our citizens have received the very pleasing information from Louis Hay, of the Townsite Company, that their agent in Sweden has organized a colony of 500 persons who will settle in Belfield and its immediate vicinity.

Mr. Ed. Gallien and family are expected to arrive from the east this evening, whither they were called by the death of Mr. Gallien's father. Mr. Brace Gallien will also return soon. These gentlemen have extensive interests here, having 100 head of cattle and about 1,500 acres of land, two or three hundred acres of which will be put under cultivation the coming season.

Belfield, unlike many other small towns, has not suffered for want of hotel accommodations. The Riverside Hotel, under the management of the enterprising and genial Max Bass, is one of the best on the line and figures very prominently as one of the important features in the development of the town.

Mr. Robt. Montgomery, or Bob. as he is familiary called, is on the sick list and his early recovery is hoped for by his many friends.

Jno. R. Thayer & Co., the popular lumber firm and contractors, will soon commence the erection of several business houses, among which will be a real estate office for Ertel & Houk.

Mr. T. J. Sharkey, traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific railroad, is in town inspecting the accounts of Mr. Frank B. B. Holmes, our accommodating station agent. Mr. Holmes' ability as a railroad man is unquestionable, and, of course, everything was found in first-class order.

Mr. F. H. Ertel is expected home from St. Paul the latter part of the week.

It is very amusing to see how enthusiastic the Dickinson people are over the proposed freight line, and our friend Scott says they are determined to push the road to completion as rapidly as time and money will permit, when we have it on good authority that they can't raise money enough to build a little bridge to enable the freighters to get out of their town. We think our sister city will soon put a damper on their enthusiasm.

The Bad Lands Cow Boy is meeting with great favor here, and the already large number of subscribers secured at this place will bear me out in this statement.

More to follow. SADIE.
articles.summary: Letter from 'Sadie' at Belfield describing the young town, a promised Swedish colony, and local comings and goings.

articles.text: The Miles City Journal has the first principles of journalistic courtesy yet to learn. It not only stole an article of ours in reference to the Bad Lands as a cattle country, but added a few lines making it applicable to the country about Miles City and published the whole as an original article, giving us not a particle of credit. Had the article appeared without any additions being made to it and no credit given to us, it would have been passed over as it might readily be an excusable mistake. The additions, however, showed that there was no mistake about the matter. It was a theft pure and simple. If the country about Miles City is so poor that it needs the aid of outside help to puff it, we would urge the cattle men to move down here. This crime of stealing articles to make up for a paucity of brains we believe should be punished by law as well as any other theft. What an editor writes is his stock in trade as much as are the goods of a merchant. The stealing of a stock in trade or any part of it is a punishable offense. Even in the short time we have been here we have repeatedly had our articles stolen, but never have we seen a more brazen-faced attempt than the one quoted above. A repetition of the offence may lead us to make a mild remonstrance. This article is merely a warning.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy accuses the Miles City Journal of lifting its Bad Lands cattle-country article without credit.

articles.text: An illustration of the stir a newspaper can make, in calling attention to the place in which it is published, is seen in the case of The Bad Lands Cow Boy. The editor of that journal, together with others who are interested in Medora, have made up their minds that the route from the Black Hills to the Northern Pacific is best which has one terminus at Medora. The Dickinson people have made up their minds that it is from their town that the most reliable, best and quickest route must start. Not until The Cow Boy started and proclaimed to the world that Medora was to be the coming headquarters of a freight to the Hills, did any one outside the little town itself dream of such a project. Now Medora is getting a deal of advertising, not merely as a point at which beeves are slaughtered, but as a point of divergence to the Hills. Concerning the merits of the two routes—that via Dickinson and that via Medora—The Pioneer has nothing to say. If our correspondents who live up the road find that we decline to publish partisan statements which they may send in to us, it is to be hoped that they will realize that The Pioneer desires to steer clear of all the rocks of discord that it can.—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprinted Mandan Pioneer comment on the Medora-Dickinson rivalry over the Black Hills freight route.

articles.text: We will now state the principal object of our making a collection of Bad Lands curiosities. We intend inside of a year to exhibit it at the Chicago exposition and perhaps at others. It will make a most interesting exhibit and will be the best possible advertisement of the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy plans to exhibit its Bad Lands curiosities at the Chicago exposition.

articles.text: This part of the country has been visited in the past few days with the most severe storm on range stock of the season. It began on Sunday morning with a slow, misty rain, which turned to ice as soon as it fell, covering ground, grass and every thing with a coating that was anything but pleasant for cattle to tackle. Sunday night and Monday it continued, changing to snow on Monday night, which continued during Tuesday and Wednesday until 10 A. M. About three inches of snow fell during that time. A strong wind Tuesday night drifted the snow into the low places, leaving the high places on the ranges covered by sleet. Yesterday about 10 o'clock the sun came out bright and shone nicely all day, melting the sleet off the high grass and making it possible for the range stock to get something to eat, the first since the storm began on Sunday morning. It is early yet to predict the result of the storm on the range below, but it is safe to say that the loss by this storm will be greater than all the previous losses this winter. Stock have suffered terribly in the last three days, and it is useless to deny the fact; but a few days of blue sky and warm south breezes will brighten up matters on the range amazingly.—Caldwell, Kan., Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped Caldwell, Kansas, report of a severe ice and snow storm on range stock.
